In [[statistics]], '''McKay's approximation''' of the [[coefficient of variation]] is a statistic based on a sample from a [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] population.  It was introduced in 1932 by A. T. McKay.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = McKay | first1 = A. T. | year = 1932 | title = Distribution of the coefficient of variation and the extended "t" distribution | journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society | volume = 95 | pages = 695–698 | doi=10.2307/2342041}}</ref> Statistical methods for the coefficient of variation often utilizes McKay's approximation.<ref>{{cite journal |jstor=1267363 |title=Comparisons of approximations to the percentage points of the sample coefficient of variation |year=1970 |last1=Iglevicz |first1=Boris |last2=Myers |first2=Raymond |journal=Technometrics |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=166–169|doi = 10.2307/1267363 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bennett | first1 = B. M. | year = 1976 | title = On an approximate test for homogeneity of coefficients of variation | journal = Contributions to Applied Statistics Dedicated to A. Linder. Experentia Suppl | volume = 22 | pages = 169–171 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |jstor=2685039 |title=Confidence intervals for a normal coefficient of variation |year=1996 |last1=Vangel |first1=Mark G. |journal=The American Statistician |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=21–26 |doi=10.1080/00031305.1996.10473537}}.</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://pub.epsilon.slu.se/4489/1/forkman_j_110214.pdf | title=Estimator and tests for common coefficients of variation in normal distributions | access-date=2013-09-23 |last1=Forkman |first1=Johannes |journal=Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods |volume=38 |pages=21–26 | doi=10.1080/03610920802187448}}</ref>

Let <math> x_i </math>, <math>i = 1, 2,\ldots, n</math> be <math> n </math> independent observations from a <math> N(\mu, \sigma^2) </math> normal distribution. The population coefficient of variation is <math> c_v = \sigma / \mu </math>. Let <math> \bar{x} </math> and <math> s \,</math> denote the [[sample mean]] and the [[sample standard deviation]], respectively. Then <math> \hat{c}_v = s/\bar{x} </math> is the sample coefficient of variation. McKay's approximation is
:<math>
K = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{c_v^2} \right) \ \frac{(n - 1) \ \hat{c}_v^2}{1 + (n - 1) \ \hat{c}_v^2/n} 
</math>
<!-- WHAT is \gamma?? -->
Note that in this expression, the first factor includes the population coefficient of variation, which is usually unknown. When <math> c_v </math> is smaller than 1/3, then <math> K </math> is approximately [[chi-squared distribution|chi-square distributed]] with <math> n - 1 </math> degrees of freedom. In the original article by McKay, the expression for <math> K </math> looks slightly different, since McKay defined <math> \sigma^2 </math> with denominator <math> n </math> instead of <math> n - 1 </math>. McKay's approximation, <math> K </math>, for the coefficient of variation is approximately chi-square distributed, but exactly [[noncentral beta distribution|noncentral beta distributed]] 
.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://pub.epsilon.slu.se/3317/1/Forkman_Verrill_080610.pdf | title=The distribution of McKay's approximation for the coefficient of variation | access-date=2013-09-23 |last1=Forkman |first1=Johannes |last2=Verrill |first2=Steve |journal=Statistics & Probability Letters |volume=78 |pages=10–14 | doi=10.1016/j.spl.2007.04.018}}</ref>
